title: 12 Best Multi-Agent Frameworks for Production in 2026

blocks.text: 12 Best Multi-Agent Frameworks for Production in 2026

LangGraph is the best multi-agent framework for production in 2026. CrewAI is the fastest path to a role-based crew, and Microsoft Agent Framework is the successor to AutoGen for Azure teams. Twelve frameworks, real tradeoffs.

LangGraph is the best multi-agent framework for production in 2026: stateful graphs, durable execution, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints, with Anthropic, Replit, LinkedIn, and Uber already shipping on it. CrewAI is the fastest path to a working crew of role-based agents. Microsoft Agent Framework is the new default for Azure and .NET teams (AutoGen is now in maintenance mode), the OpenAI Agents SDK fits OpenAI-first stacks, the Claude Agent SDK fits teams building on Claude, and AWS Multi-Agent Orchestrator (renamed Agent Squad) fits Bedrock shops.

The trap: many "frameworks" are wrappers around a single LLM call with a planner prompt. Real orchestrators handle concurrency, retries, durable state, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and the names in marketing decks are not always the names that show up in stable production stacks. In 2026, the framework you pick decides whether the system survives production or stays a prototype.

This guide compares the 12 best multi-agent frameworks for production in 2026. Real capabilities, honest pricing where it is publicly known, pros and cons, who should skip each one, and 4 questions that pick the right one for your stack.

How we ranked them. Production readiness counts most: durable state, human-in-the-loop, and tracing. Then the orchestration patterns each framework ships, then how active the maintainers are, then lock-in. Facts come from each project's official docs and GitHub repo. The two entries added in this update (Microsoft Agent Framework and the Claude Agent SDK) were checked against their docs on 2026-09-26. We did not run a benchmark for this list, so no hands-on testing is claimed.
Best multi-agent frameworks: a brief overview
LangGraph: Best for production-grade stateful agent graphs with human-in-the-loop checkpoints, used by Anthropic, Replit, LinkedIn, Uber.
CrewAI: Best for role-based agent crews with the lowest barrier to entry; the fastest path from idea to working swarm.
Microsoft Agent Framework: Best for Azure and .NET teams that want graph workflows with sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, and manager-led patterns built in.
AutoGen (Microsoft): Best for conversational multi-agent research on existing AutoGen code; new projects should start on Microsoft Agent Framework.
OpenAI Swarm / Agents SDK: Best for teams already deep in the OpenAI ecosystem who want lightweight handoffs.
Claude Agent SDK: Best for Claude-based agents that delegate to parallel subagents with their own tools, prompts, and models.
Multi-Agent Orchestrator (now Agent Squad): Best for AWS-native production deployments with Bedrock and Lambda.
MetaGPT: Best for simulating software engineering teams (PM, architect, dev, QA) end-to-end.
AgentScope (Alibaba): Best for high-throughput distributed agent systems with strong observability.
AGiXT: Best for self-hosted, plugin-heavy agent platforms with a UI for non-engineers.
SuperAGI: Best for autonomous agent workflows with built-in GUI, memory, and toolkits.
Google ADK: Best for Gemini-native production agents with graph workflows and native MCP tools.
1. LangGraph, best for production-grade stateful agents

LangGraph is the orchestration framework from the LangChain team, and by 2026 it is the de facto standard for serious multi-agent systems. Unlike LangChain itself, LangGraph is purpose-built for graph-structured agent flows with persistent state, conditional edges, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and durable execution. It is the framework behind agents shipped by Anthropic, Replit, LinkedIn, Uber, Elastic, and a growing list of Fortune 500 deployments documented in LangChain case studies.

The reason LangGraph wins production over flashier alternatives is mundane: it treats agents as state machines, not chat loops. You define nodes, edges, and a shared state schema. The runtime handles persistence, replay, time-travel debugging, and interruption, the unglamorous primitives that decide whether your agent survives the first 10,000 real users. Pair LangGraph with LangSmith for tracing and you get the closest thing to a production-ready multi-agent stack the open ecosystem currently ships.
Key features
Stateful agent graphs with typed shared state
Durable execution with checkpointers (Postgres, Redis, SQLite)
Human-in-the-loop interrupts and time-travel debugging
Streaming, tool calling, and subgraph composition
First-class TypeScript and Python SDKs
Best for
Teams shipping agents to real users at scale
Workflows that need human approval mid-execution
Long-running agents that must survive process restarts
Pricing
Framework itself is open source (MIT)
LangSmith observability is paid (Plus tier from $39/user/month, Enterprise custom)
Pros
Production-tested by Anthropic, Replit, LinkedIn, Uber
The strongest debugging story on this list via the LangSmith trace UI
Durable state means agents survive crashes
Strong community and frequent releases
Cons
Steeper learning curve than CrewAI or Swarm
Tight coupling to LangChain ecosystem (some teams want a leaner stack)
Free weekly brief
Steal our production automations
The exact n8n flows, Claude Code setups, and prompts we ship for clients, broken down step by step. No spam, unsubscribe anytime.
2. CrewAI, best for role-based agent crews

CrewAI hit the multi-agent scene in late 2023 and by 2026 it is the most popular framework for teams who want a working multi-agent system in an afternoon, not a quarter. Its core abstraction, "crews" of role-based agents with goals, backstories, and assigned tasks, maps cleanly to how non-engineers think about delegating work. You define a Researcher, an Analyst, a Writer; CrewAI handles the handoffs.

CrewAI's enterprise tier added in 2024-2025 has pulled it into real production use beyond demos. Teams use it for content pipelines, sales research, internal ops bots, and customer support triage. It is not as low-level or as debuggable as LangGraph, but for 70% of real business workflows that gap does not matter.
Key features
Role/goal/backstory agent definitions
Sequential and hierarchical crew processes
Built-in tool integrations (Serper, browsing, RAG)
CrewAI Enterprise for hosted execution and monitoring
Python-first with a growing CLI
Best for
Business workflows with clear role separation
Teams without deep ML/agent engineering experience
Rapid prototyping and demoable proofs
Pricing
Open source core (MIT)
CrewAI Enterprise tier with hosted runtime and observability (custom pricing)
Pros
Fastest path from idea to working crew
Excellent docs and templates
Active community on YouTube and GitHub
Enterprise tier closes the production gap
Cons
Less control over low-level execution than LangGraph
Hierarchical mode can be opaque to debug at scale
3. Microsoft Agent Framework, best for Azure and .NET multi-agent workflows

Microsoft Agent Framework is the direct successor to both AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, built by the same teams. Microsoft's docs describe it as combining AutoGen's simple agent abstractions with Semantic Kernel's enterprise features (session-based state, type safety, middleware, telemetry) and adding graph-based workflows for explicit multi-agent orchestration. If you are starting a new Microsoft-stack agent project today, this is where Microsoft points you.

The multi-agent story is concrete. Workflows ship five built-in orchestration patterns: sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, and Magentic, where a manager agent coordinates specialists. Orchestrations can pause on approval-required tools for human review. The GitHub README lists checkpointing, streaming, human-in-the-loop, and time-travel, plus built-in OpenTelemetry tracing, which covers most of what separates a production system from a demo.
Key features
Graph-based workflows with sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, and Magentic orchestration
Checkpointing, streaming, human-in-the-loop, and time-travel
Built-in OpenTelemetry integration for tracing
MCP client support for tools
Python and C#/.NET with consistent APIs; Go in public preview
Model providers include Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama
Best for
Azure and .NET shops building new multi-agent systems
Teams migrating off AutoGen or Semantic Kernel (official migration guides exist for both)
Workflows that need explicit, auditable execution paths between agents
Pricing
Open source (MIT)
You pay for model usage and any Azure services you deploy on
Pros
Official successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, so it is where Microsoft's agent investment now goes
Five orchestration patterns out of the box instead of hand-rolled routing
OpenTelemetry tracing built in, not bolted on
Same concepts in Python and .NET
Cons
Young as a merged framework: some .NET packages still install with a prerelease flag, and the Go SDK is in public preview without functional workflows
Documentation and samples lean on Microsoft Foundry and Azure, even though other providers are supported
Skip it if you have no Microsoft footprint and already run LangGraph in production. You would trade a proven checkpointing story for a newer one without gaining much.
4. AutoGen (Microsoft), best for conversational multi-agent research

AutoGen, originally from Microsoft Research, popularized the "agents that talk to each other" paradigm in 2023 and matured with its v0.4 architecture rewrite. It is the framework many academic papers and Microsoft-internal projects build on, and it ships with deep Azure OpenAI integration out of the box. One change matters for any production decision: the AutoGen GitHub README now says the project "is now in maintenance mode" and "will not receive new features or enhancements," and it points new users to Microsoft Agent Framework (entry 3).

The v0.4 architecture introduced an event-driven core with actor-style messaging, making AutoGen more suitable for distributed deployments than its earlier conversation-loop design. For research teams and Azure-native enterprises it remains a top pick, particularly for scenarios involving code execution, group chat patterns, and tool-using assistants that need to negotiate.
Key features
Event-driven, actor-style agent runtime (v0.4+)
Group chat, nested chat, and sequential patterns
AutoGen Studio low-code UI for prototyping
Strong code-execution sandbox support
Tight integration with Azure OpenAI and Semantic Kernel
Best for
Research teams exploring agent communication patterns
Azure-native enterprises
Code-generation and code-review multi-agent setups
Pricing
Fully open source (MIT/CC-BY-4.0)
LLM costs via Azure OpenAI or other providers
Pros
Built by Microsoft Research, with a large body of papers and samples
Excellent for code-executing agents
AutoGen Studio lowers the bar for non-coders
Official migration guide to Microsoft Agent Framework when you outgrow it
Cons
In maintenance mode: no new features, community managed going forward
Breaking changes between v0.2 and v0.4 hurt some teams
Less opinionated than LangGraph, so production patterns vary
5. OpenAI Agents SDK (formerly Swarm), best for OpenAI-native handoffs

OpenAI shipped Swarm as an experimental framework in late 2024 and graduated it into the production-ready OpenAI Agents SDK in 2025. The design philosophy is intentionally minimalist: agents, tools, and handoffs. Nothing else. No graph DSL, no orchestration ceremony, just a clean Python API that mirrors how the OpenAI Assistants and Responses APIs already think about delegation.

For teams already deep in the OpenAI ecosystem (using GPT-4.1, the Responses API, function calling, and the assistants platform) the Agents SDK is the path of least resistance. It does not try to be a universal orchestrator. It tries to be the most ergonomic way to build agent swarms on top of OpenAI's own runtime, and it succeeds at that.
Key features
Minimal API: agents, tools, handoffs
Native Responses API integration
Built-in tracing in the OpenAI dashboard
Guardrails and structured outputs
Python SDK with a JS port maturing
Best for
OpenAI-first teams
Lightweight agent handoff use cases
Teams allergic to framework bloat
Pricing
SDK is free and open source
Pay-as-you-go OpenAI API usage
Pros
Cleanest API of any framework in this list
Zero migration cost if you already use OpenAI
Official OpenAI tracing dashboard
Production-ready as of late 2025
Cons
Single-provider lock-in (OpenAI only by default)
No durable state; long-running agents need external persistence
6. Claude Agent SDK, best for Claude-based agents that delegate to subagents

The Claude Agent SDK is Anthropic's library for building agents on the same agent loop, built-in tools, and context management that run Claude Code, programmable in Python and TypeScript. It replaced the earlier Claude Code SDK packages (Anthropic publishes a migration guide). Its multi-agent model is subagents: a main agent spawns separate agent instances for focused subtasks, and each one runs in its own conversation.

That design solves the problem that kills most multi-agent builds, which is context bloat. Per Anthropic's docs, only a subagent's final message returns to the parent, so a research subagent can read dozens of files without flooding the main agent. Subagents can run concurrently, each with its own system prompt, tool allowlist, and model. You can cap nesting depth, concurrent subagents, and total spend per query, and a Workflow tool in the TypeScript SDK moves larger runs of many agents into a script.
Key features
Subagents defined in code or as markdown files in .claude/agents/
Per-subagent system prompt, tool allowlist, and model override
Parallel subagents with isolated context; subagents can spawn their own
Caps on subagent depth, concurrency, and dollar spend per query
Built-in tools, hooks, permissions, sessions, and MCP connections
Best for
Coding, code review, and repo-level ops agents
Teams already standardized on Claude
Research and audit agents that read far more than they return
Pricing
No separate license fee; usage is billed through the Claude API
Governed by Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service rather than an open-source license
Pros
Same agent loop and tools that run Claude Code, so you are not assembling a harness from scratch
Context isolation per subagent keeps the parent agent's window small
Spend and concurrency caps give you a hard ceiling on runaway agent trees
Tool allowlists per subagent limit what each agent can touch
Cons
Built around Claude models, so it is a single-vendor choice like the OpenAI Agents SDK
Delegation is model-driven: Claude decides when to spawn subagents, so you get less explicit routing than a LangGraph graph or a Microsoft Agent Framework workflow

Skip it if your agents must run on several model vendors, or your process needs fixed, auditable step order. A graph framework fits that better. For a deeper comparison with the CLI, see Claude Agent SDK vs Claude Code.
7. AWS Multi-Agent Orchestrator (now Agent Squad), best for AWS-native deployments

AWS released the Multi-Agent Orchestrator in 2024 as an open-source framework for routing user queries across specialized agents on Amazon Bedrock. It has since been renamed Agent Squad, and its GitHub README now says the project moved from awslabs to 2fastlabs/agent-squad, where it is maintained today. It is still the most natural fit for teams already running on AWS who want multi-agent systems without leaving the AWS ecosystem.

The framework's intent classification layer, which routes incoming requests to the right specialized agent, is what sets it apart. It plugs directly into Bedrock, Lambda, and Amazon API Gateway, and ships Python and TypeScript implementations (the current README adds Swift). A SupervisorAgent lets a lead agent direct specialist agents in parallel. For enterprises with strict data residency and AWS-only mandates, this is the most natural multi-agent stack on the market.
Key features
Intent classifier routes queries to specialized agents
Native Bedrock, Lambda, and Anthropic Claude integration
Conversation memory in DynamoDB
